I'm writing this to document my experience as a CCA in Nov/Dec 2016 as I'm sure prospective employees would like to know what they're getting in to. I used to enviously watch the mailman leisurely saunter down the street in the sunshine and think it was the dream job. Why not give it a shot? Before I applied to USPS, I had read all the horror stories online. I naively dismissed them as whining from lazy, fat asses who would shudder at the thought of exercise. I'm in good shape and enjoy cycling and outdoor activities - "I'll be fine" I thought.

A month after my initial application for the job, I was invited to take a drug test and interview. Another few weeks later, I was invited for orientation (sitting in a classroom watching endless powerpoint slides), carrier academy (some hands on training) and driving school. This was strike one against the post office - it's a bureaucratic nightmare and everything takes forever to organize. However, you get paid for all the training so I couldn't complain too much.

Feeling confident and prepared, I show up for my first day at my local station at 8am. The supervisor acts surprised to see me. There is supposed to be an instructor to accompany me for my first 3 days but one hasn't be assigned. I am sent home and told to come back in two hours. The shoddiness of their organization wasn't the best first impression. "What have I got myself into" I mutter to myself. I return later and head out on a route with my instructor to deliver the mail. There is a lot of walking but that doesn't bother me. I'm making mental notes of everything my instructor is telling me - what to do with certified mail, getting signatures, scanning parcels. At the end of the 3 days, my feet are covered in blisters and my back aches but I continue to trudge on as I believe it'll get easier. (Spoiler: it doesn't).

From then on, I'm on my own. Each day I was given a new route to cover which made it impossible to adjust to a routine. Some days were okay (driving routes were I leaned out the truck to deliver mail) while others were hellish (delivering to businesses along a busy main street where parking was difficult). I was using my phone's GPS to navigate a lot of time which drained the battery. I was under constant stress to get everything delivered and return to the station on time. On really long days, my scanner's battery died meaning I had to use my phone to take pictures of the barcode so I could scan them later. Often I was delivering after dark which made reading addresses a nightmare. I never once had time to take the designated 30 min lunch break (it's deducted from your wages regardless) and still I was never fast enough for the supervisors.

The breaking point was about two weeks into the job. After an exceedingly long day, I return to the station hungry, tired, covered in sweat and with a few parcels destined for businesses that I couldn't deliver because they were closed. One of the supervisors starts roaring that I should have been finished two hours ago. When you bust your ass all day and hear that crap you begin to wonder "what's the point". There are easier ways to make a dollar. The next morning, I handed in my resignation. The supervisor didn't seemed surprised. He recited a rehearsed exit speech that I'm sure he has given hundreds of times to all the new applicants who quickly get fed up.

Apparently a staggering 70% of new CCAs quit within the first year. Now I know why. My advice to USPS is go easy on the noobs at the start. Try to keep them on the same route for a week or two. Allow them extra time. Hire supervisors who aren't dicks. My advice to anyone thinking of joining USPS is don't do it. Ignore this wisdom (like I did!) at your own peril. Seeing how much of the mail is junk advertisements or bank statements that should be paperless is depressing. You're busting your ass to deliver mail nobody wants in the first place. It's the 21st century - use email. The post office won't survive the next 50 years and I will take pleasure in its demise.
